links.note: The Greek adjective “sheep” implies a gate here.
Greek says “having his illness”; English describes the man as sick.
English supplies the illness from the preceding description.
The article introduces “the one”; English says “him who.”
English repeats the mat already named in the preceding command.
Greek uses the article as a pronoun; English names Jesus.
Greek says “answered and was saying”; English compresses both verbs.
English names the implied sender as “my Father.”
English makes “testimony” the subject and adds a relative clause.
The Greek genitive expresses comparison: “than John’s.”
English supplies a relative clause where Greek repeats the article.
Greek says “you have hoped”; English expands the verb.
